title: The graded stabilizer ideal forces opposite-degree products to generate one
statement: Let $M$ be an abelian group, written additively, and $A$ a commutative ring with additive subgroups $A_m\subseteq A$ such that every element is a unique finite sum of elements of the $A_m$, $1\in A_0$, and $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$. Thus $A=\bigoplus_{m\in M}A_m$ is an $M$-graded ring. Let $A[M]$ be the ring of finite formal sums $\sum_m c_mt^m$, with $c_m\in A$ and $t^mt^n=t^{m+n}$; the coefficient grading of $A$ is independent of these formal symbols. Let $I\subseteq A[M]$ be the ideal generated by $a(t^m-1)$ for all $m\in M$ and $a\in A_m$, and let $J\subseteq A[M]$ be the ideal generated by all $t^m-1$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. If $I=J$, then for every $m\in M$ there are finitely many $a_j\in A_m$ and $b_j\in A_{-m}$ such that $\sum_j a_jb_j=1$. Empty finite sums are allowed when $A$ is the zero ring.

source.place: Tag 0EKK (lemma-complete-reducibility-Gm) gives the grading interpretation. The augmentation-ideal auxiliary is formulated and proved independently by Q20 in report.md; it is not asserted verbatim in 0EKK. It algebraically supplies the homogeneous-unit step of Abramovich--Temkin, Luna’s fundamental lemma for diagonalizable groups, Lemma 5.4.4, whose local copy is WANTED.

proof.text: Fix $m$. If $A=0$, use the empty sum. Otherwise put $B=A_0$ and let $K\subseteq B$ consist of finite sums $\sum_j a_jb_j$ with $a_j\in A_m$, $b_j\in A_{-m}$. This is an ideal: additive inverses can be absorbed into $a_j$, and $c a_j\in A_m$ for $c\in B$. Suppose $1\notin K$. Let $L=KA$ be the ideal of finite sums $\sum_i k_i x_i$ with $k_i\in K$, $x_i\in A$. Its degree-$n$ component is $\sum_i k_i(x_i)_n$, so $L$ is homogeneous and its degree-zero component lies in $K$. Hence $1\notin L$.

source.place: Tag 0EKK (lemma-complete-reducibility-Gm), grading context only; independent Q112 refinement of the Q20 algebraic proof retained in coord/reports/Q20/lem-sfb-affine-free-split-torus-invariants.md.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-homogeneous-maximal-graded-field-quotient] to this proper homogeneous ideal $L$. Obtain $q:A\to D=A/H$ with $L\subseteq H$, $D\ne0$, $D_n=q(A_n)$, and every nonzero element of $D_n$ invertible by an element of $D_{-n}$.

source.place: Tag 0EKK (lemma-complete-reducibility-Gm), grading context only; independent Q112 refinement of the Q20 algebraic proof retained in coord/reports/Q20/lem-sfb-affine-free-split-torus-invariants.md.

proof.text: Put $N=\{n\in M:D_n\ne0\}$. It contains $0$ since $1\ne0$. It is closed under negatives by the homogeneous inverse assertion of [lem-sfb-homogeneous-maximal-graded-field-quotient], and under addition because a product of two units is a nonzero unit. Thus $N$ is a subgroup of $M$.

source.place: Tag 0EKK (lemma-complete-reducibility-Gm), grading context only; independent Q112 refinement of the Q20 algebraic proof retained in coord/reports/Q20/lem-sfb-affine-free-split-torus-invariants.md.

proof.text: Let $E$ be the ring of finite formal sums $\sum_{\gamma\in M/N}d_\gamma u^\gamma$ over $D$, with $u^\gamma u^\delta=u^{\gamma+\delta}$. Define $\Phi:A[M]\to E$ by $\Phi(\sum_r c_rt^r)=\sum_r q(c_r)u^{r+N}$. Finite distributivity and $q(cc\prime)=q(c)q(c\prime)$ show that this is a ring map. For a generator $a(t^n-1)$ of $I$, either $q(a)=0$, or $n\in N$ and $u^{n+N}=1$; in both cases its image is zero. Therefore $I\subseteq\ker\Phi$. Since $I=J$, every $t^r-1$ maps to zero. If $r\notin N$, the coefficient of $u^{r+N}$ in $u^{r+N}-1$ is $1_D\ne0$, a contradiction. Consequently $N=M$.

source.place: Tag 0EKK (lemma-complete-reducibility-Gm), grading context only; independent Q112 refinement of the Q20 algebraic proof retained in coord/reports/Q20/lem-sfb-affine-free-split-torus-invariants.md.

proof.text: Choose nonzero $d\in D_m$ and its inverse $e\in D_{-m}$ from [lem-sfb-homogeneous-maximal-graded-field-quotient]. Lift them to $a\in A_m$, $b\in A_{-m}$. Then $ab\in K\subseteq L\subseteq H$, so the quotient-kernel assertion of [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient] gives $de=q(ab)=0$, contradicting $de=1\ne0$. Thus $1\in K$, which is exactly the required finite sum of opposite-degree products.
